changes.text: A meadow, a river, and trees good for food take shape.
The Tree of Life and the Tree of Knowledge stand at the garden's heart.
Birds, a lamb, and drifting light fill it with quiet life.
Adam — or Eve — can walk the garden for the first time.
Eve joins Adam in the garden; the other always wanders nearby.
A word of welcome now greets every visitor at the gate.
The river parts east of the garden into four heads, fanning through the mist.
Five fish — one gold — swim and rise in the shallows.
A whole day now passes in seven minutes, morning to starlit night.
The moon takes the light after the sun sets.
Four standing stones name the river's heads: Pishon, Gihon, Tigris, Euphrates.
The garden finds its voice: wind, water, birdsong, and crickets, woven live.
Doves and cattle graze and roost beside the lamb.
A morning mist rises to water the ground.
The night sky bears its signs: the Bear, Orion, and the Pleiades.
Drawing near the Tree of Life kindles a quiet reverence.
Sound becomes opt-in, and the garden's voice is gentled.
Draw near any creature and its Hebrew name is given — Taleh the lamb, Yonah the dove, and more.
Clouds cast real shade, and a gentle rain sometimes passes over.
The night sky wheels slowly through the seasons of a long year.
Butterflies and bees fill the flowers, each named as they're found.

log.focus: stillness, the banks, and the east

changes.text: Stand still by the water and the shyer creatures draw near.
Reeds grow soft along the river's banks.
A gate of pale stone stands far to the east, a hush of what will keep the way.
Something unnamed stirs the grass near the Tree of Knowledge, and is gone.
The river takes on the hour's colour, and the banks reflect in it.
Every step through the water leaves a widening ring.
Petals drift from the trees and settle into the grass.
Dew gathers overnight and glints at first light.
Two sweeps of light gather above the eastern gate at dawn — the keeper, still hinted, never shown.
At evening a wind moves through the garden, and the trees bow as it passes.
West of the garden, the river is found rising among wet stones.
Figs and pomegranates ripen on a few trees, named as you draw near.
The lamb finds two companions, and the cattle low softly at dusk.
Footprints linger a while in the sandy banks, then fade.
Fallen fig leaves lie sewn together at the foot of the dark tree.
Gold, bdellium, and onyx glint among the stones where the Pishon runs.
The birds nest in the sacred trees' branches, and in time a chick or two of their own.
On the seventh day the garden keeps a deeper rest — even the wind at peace.
The Tree of Life bears its own fruit in season, not just gold leaves.
At first light the morning stars sing together, just before the day quiets them.
A tree stands apart at the river's bank, its leaf never withering, fruited every season.
The valleys fill with grain, swaying together the moment the evening wind walks through.
Goats keep the rising rim, sure-footed among the high stones.
An eagle circles high above the garden, and makes her nest higher still.
A hart keeps the riverside, panting after the water brooks.

log.focus: after the rain, and the small and slow

changes.text: The rain leaves the sky clear and blue behind it, cloud by cloud, once its hour has passed.
Sit still by the water a while, and the nearest lamb comes to lie down beside it.
A stork keeps her nest high in her own fir tree, above every other nest in the garden.
Locusts go forth by bands across the meadow, no king leading any of them.
A creeping thing keeps close to the ground by the water's edge, slowest of all.
After the shower, low puddles glisten a while before the ground drinks them in.
Wildflowers dot the meadow grass in quick dabs of color among the green.
A wild ass ranges far and free over the plain, keeping its own distance from every path.
The hart's fawn keeps close beside her, unsteady but quick to follow.
A rainbow eases faintly into the clearing sky once a shower has passed.
A lion keeps company with the flock and lies down among them, and the fear between them is not yet.
Cedars of Lebanon stand tall and full of sap along the garden's northern rim.
Webs strung in the meadow grass show themselves only while the morning dew is on them.
A sparrow and a swallow keep the sacred trees' nests, off on short errands and always home again.
The moon waxes and wanes through the same twenty-eight days the signs take to wheel full circle.
The garden's shadows draw out long toward evening and swing round with the sun.
Willows lean over the brook along the one wide stretch, their fronds hanging to the water.
At evening a covey of quail comes up low over the meadow and settles into the grass till the dew lifts.
Ants keep one worn road between their hill and the grain, out empty and back laden, with no one directing them.
The evening star follows the sun down, alight over the west before any other star is given.
Every grazing creature rebuilt to a quarter of its old drawing cost, so the garden has room to grow again.
A skein of cranes crosses high overhead each morning, keeping their own appointed time.
Conies keep their houses among the high rocks beside the goats, and duck from sight now and then.
A vine has climbed one of the garden's trees, its clusters hanging low and ready.
At evening the loosened leaves scud before the same wind that bows the trees.
Here and there a palm tree stands, flourishing the way the righteous are said to.
A wolf lies down beside the lamb, and neither is afraid.
Almond branches blossom white on the eastern rise, first to wake of all the trees.
The turtledove's voice sounds again, answering the same wind that bows the trees.
Frankincense trees stand fragrant on the garden's warmer western slope.
Hyssop springs up among the high rocks, least of all the garden's trees.
White lilies keep the garden's rougher ground, each stand ringed by the thorns it came up through.
A raven drops to whichever provision is next in turn, is fed there, and lifts off again.
One fig tree keeps the long year rather than the day: bare, then tender, then full-leafed as summer draws near.
Camphire blooms in clusters, stirring on the same evening wind the turtledove answers.
Vapours ascend off the water and the warm ground through the heat of the middle day.
Beside every stand of briars a myrtle or a fir has come up, and the thorns are left standing under them.
Two little foxes keep the vine, circling it in the low light and stopping to nose at the clusters.
Bound sheaves stand upright at the edge of both fields, where the corn has been cut.
Hoarfrost lies scattered like ashes over the grass through the last watch of the coldest turn of the year.
The hart breaks off grazing on her own long thirst, goes down to the bank to drink, and her fawn goes with her.
The fir by the nest, the tree by the waters, the gateway's stone and both sacred trees each bake into one geometry — seventeen draw calls given back to the garden's budget.
An olive stands apart on the south-west meadow, and one dove leaves the circuit now and then to go down to it and carry a leaf home in her mouth.
Springs break out of the rim and run down among the hills, each finding its own way by the fall of the land — some to a channel of the river, some into a hollow of the meadow.
Mandrakes keep the ground under the vine, and give their smell through the warm of the afternoon into the evening.
Behemoth lies down on a bank the willows compass about, and does nothing all day but breathe and lift his head to the water.
While the sun is low the crowns part the light instead of stopping it, and shafts of it lie out long across the grass.

log.focus: the night watch, and the ram

changes.text: An owl keeps the night watch high in the cedars of the northern rim, turning her head and doing nothing else, and she is gone by morning — and each night she takes a different tree.
Of the five springs, one finds the great river; where it goes over the lip a ring widens out into the channel and a ring comes answering back, and neither of them stops.
A ram stands caught by his horns in a thicket on the eastern rim. He leans back against it now and then, finds it still has him, and goes on cropping — he was never frightened, only held.
A poplar, a hazel and a chestnut stand together over the watering place on the river's north bank, with peeled rods set in the shallows below them, white where the bark was taken off.
The meadow stands full of seed, and it is brushing past a head — not the hour, not the evening gust — that looses the down off it and sends it up.
Both wings of every bird in the garden now share one instanced mesh, which gives seven draw calls back to the budget before any of the above is spent.

log.focus: there is hope of a tree

changes.text: A vine no one planted has run out along the open meadow — three runners going out from one old root, taking hold again at every few nodes, and putting out tendrils for something to climb that was never set there.

Every coney now has the house the proverb gives it: a knot of rock standing behind it, a dark gap at the foot of it, and the threshold across that gap worn pale by a feeble folk going in and out of it.
At evening the swallows come down onto the river and work it end to end in long low beats, and at the bottom of each beat one of them touches the water and leaves a ring widening behind it.
A bed of grey-green bushes keeps a slope on the south that falls away to the sun, and through the noon its smell flows out — northward, off the warm ground and away over the meadow.

One tree in the garden is down, and out of the rim of the broken stock, close enough to the river to be within the scent of the water, tender shoots have come up. Through the whole turn of the year they thicken and draw back, but they never quite cease.
All six butterflies now share one instanced mesh for their twelve wings and another for their bodies, which gives sixteen draw calls back to the budget before any of the above is spent.

On the south-western rim a rock goes up in ledges like a stair, and a dove keeps the cleft near the top of it. From the meadow she is hardly there; come up to the foot of the stair and she steps out to the lip of her ledge, turns her face to you, and calls once.

In the heaviest of a shower, lightning is now and then kindled far off past the rim and the garden is lit by it for a moment — and the thunder comes a while after, softer and later the farther off it struck.

An ostrich ranges the whole south of the garden at a run, stands a while and pecks wherever she fetches up, and runs on. Her eggs lie half sunk in the warm dust of a scrape on the open meadow, and once every round she goes straight past them without slowing.
As the evening wind goes through, every tree in the meadow shivers quickly on top of its slow lean, each to its own beat, and the leaves are heard striking together in short dry claps.

High on the warm shoulder of the dove's rock, wild bees have built in a hollow: pale-gold combs hang in the dark of it, the honey has run down over the lip of the stone, and the bees work the air in front of it by day.

Adam no longer walks faster or slower with every small movement of the thumb. Any drag is one steady walk, and only a drag pushed clearly out — or Shift on a keyboard — quickens him into a longer stride; whichever pace it is, it holds for as long as the finger does.
A drag or a key to the right now turns him to the right. Ever since the garden was first walked, right and left had been swapped on the screen, so he went off the opposite way to the thumb.

A long drag no longer runs the thumb off the edge of the screen: the place it started now follows on behind the finger, and his heading is eased, so a nervous thumb no longer zigzags him across the grass.

The view swings round behind him more slowly than he turns, so a drag held to one side carves a wide, calm curve — about a quarter of the old turning rate — instead of spinning him on the spot; and a drag back toward the view walks him straight back toward it, where before it only turned him round and round where he stood.
He slows to wade only in the river itself. The low dry hollows of the meadow used to slow him too, so his pace seemed to change for no reason on open grass.

South of the meadow's heart a mustard has grown past every herb round it into a tree — many stems out of one root, a broad low crown yellow with its own small flowers — and the birds of the air lodge in it, turning on their twigs and hopping now and then from one to another.

The eagle's nest now stands on a crag of its own on the south-western rim, with two young in it. Before she leaves them in the morning, and once on every round of her day's circuit, she comes down and hangs over the nest beating her spread wings, and the young stretch up toward her until she goes.

As the dew goes up in the morning, small white rounds are found lying in patches over the meadow, and by the heat of the noon they have melted away. Come up to a patch and it is named; on the seventh day there is none.
The long year now has its two seasons of rain: the first rain in the autumn turn and the latter rain in the spring, when the dry spells between showers shorten and the showers themselves run longer.
Whenever a lamb sets out across the meadow it goes the first few strides in skips, all four feet off the grass at once, before it settles into a walk.

Tap the ground and Adam walks there and stops on the spot, so a long walk no longer means holding a drag the whole way. A faint ring lies on the grass where the tap fell and fades as he arrives; any drag or key takes back over at once.
Sent toward a creature (or anything else that has a name), he stops of his own accord once he has come up beside it and its name is given, instead of walking on through it to the ground behind.
Letting go now stops him within a short step. Before, he slid on for half a stride with his legs still swinging.
Asked to go to the side or back the way he came, he turns before he strides off, instead of wheeling away in a wide loop in whatever direction he happened to be facing.

A stair of rough ledges now climbs the face of the eagle's crag that looks into the garden, and a hind keeps it. She grazes at the foot, then goes up ledge by ledge in short, sure leaps, stands longest at the top looking out over the whole garden, and picks her way down again. Come up to her and she is named.
The grain keeps the long year: green after the first rain, ripening to gold once the latter rain has fallen, and standing pale, white to harvest, through the summer.
After a shower the grass of the meadow stands greener and brighter for a while, then slowly settles back as the ground dries. The sand and the stone stay as they were.
Three shittah trees stand on the dry southern rim, each a short grey trunk forked low under a broad, flat crown, wider than the tree is tall. Each is named when he comes near.

log.focus: to dress it and to keep it

changes.text: Here and there on the meadow, a short walk up from the river, lies a patch of bare, dry ground. Wade into the river, or stand a moment at its edge, and Adam takes up water in his cupped hands and carries it; walk to a dry patch and stand still on it, and he lets it go. A mist goes up off the ground, and the patch greens and comes into flower.
The garden remembers his work. A patch he has watered stays green for a day, even if he leaves the garden and comes back, then slowly goes back to dry ground over the next, ready to be watered again.

The eagle's crag, the dove's stepped rock and the conies' houses are solid now. He no longer walks through the middle of them: walking into the side of one, he slides on round it, and a tap on the far side walks him round the rock to the place.
Stepping up onto the stones of the crossing, or down off them into the water, now reads as a step. Before, his whole body jumped up or dropped by half his own height in a single moment.
In the water his stride changes as well as his pace: a slower, shorter, higher-kneed step pushed through the current, leaning into it, with his arms lifted a little out to his sides.

Clumps of flag stand up out of the mire in the shallows of the slow western reach, tall flat leaves with a bud on each stalk, and in their spring season, after the latter rain, the buds open blue. Wade up to a clump and it is named.

The hind on the crag's stair has a fawn of her own. It keeps one ledge below her as she climbs, following each of her leaps a moment after she lands in a slower, higher leap of its own, and grazes at her side at the foot. It is named when he comes near.
The shallows of the slow reach swarm with fry: a few small shoals wheeling just under the surface. Wade in among one and it scatters all at once, then slowly draws together again.

The ground blossoms wherever he walks. Flowers spring up out of the grass and the sand round his feet as he goes, open wide, and stand open behind him for half a minute and more, so he can turn and see the way he came written across the meadow in colour. Then each closes back into a bud and sinks into the grass again.
Stand still in the open and the blossoming spreads out from him in a widening ring, so even a visitor who has not yet moved arrives to flowers opening round them.
The one who walks with him leaves a lighter trail of flowers of their own wherever they wander.
As the flowers open, a soft note sounds now and then, wandering a step or two at a time into a slow tune; standing still, the notes climb as the ring spreads.
After dark the open flowers keep a faint light of their own, so the way he has walked glows on the meadow at night.
All of it is one draw call: each flower's whole life, from rising to sinking, is worked out on the graphics chip from the moment it was born.

log.focus: behold the fowls of the air

changes.text: A great flock of small birds keeps the garden's sky: more than a thousand of them wheeling together as one body, a swirling cloud that tilts and folds, stretches into a long ribbon and gathers into a ball, with dark waves rolling through it.
Stand still and look, and the flock leaves its own wandering and comes to wheel low over the meadow just before you, and as it comes its name is given.
Close by, the rush of all those wings is heard, swelling with each wave through the flock.

It keeps its own day: up out of the reeds at first light, off beyond the rim through the heat of the middle day, back out of the westering sun to dance against the evening sky, then down into the reeds by the river, bird by bird, as the light goes.
All of it is one draw call: where every bird flies, how it beats its wings and when it drops into the reeds is worked out on the graphics chip, and each bird turns to show the watcher its wings.

log.focus: a pure river of water of life

changes.text: The river comes alive with light: by day the sun lays a glittering path across it, a host of tiny glints flashing and dancing on the ripples, shifting as you move.
Under the moon the same path shines silver, brighter as she waxes full.
At night the water carries a soft light of its own, pale pulses drifting downstream; wade in and it brightens round your legs and lies glowing behind you where you have walked, and its name is given.
Now and then, as the water lights round you, it answers with a soft high note.
Stand a moment under a fig or a pomegranate in fruit and a ripe one drops, turning, into your hands, freely given.
He holds it up to look at it, eats it in three bites, and his hands are free again; walk out from under the tree and come back, and it gives again.
All of the river's light is one draw call: whether each glint catches the sun or the moon is worked out on the graphics chip from where the watcher stands.

A flock of its own now grazes the meadow between the two great trees, straight ahead of where every visit begins: ewes and their lambs, heads down in the grass, wandering a few steps to fresh grazing, round the trunks and never through them.

Walk in among them and they know him: each one near lifts its head and falls in behind, and any grazing beside one that has joined comes too, so a walk through the flock gathers it, and its name is given.
They follow the very way he went, round the rock where he went round it, strung out behind him; the lambs frisk to keep up.
Stand still and they come up round him; stand a little longer and they lie down at his feet, and the psalm's word is given.
They will not wade: go into the river and they wait at the brink, drinking, until he comes back, or until he has gone so far that they let him go.
Wherever he leads them becomes their pasture, and the garden remembers it, so next visit the flock is grazing where he left it.
Through the heat of the middle day, and through the night, the grazing flock lies down where it is.
A shepherd's pipe plays as they come: a breathy note as each sheep falls in, and a slow tune while the flock walks behind him.
All fourteen sheep are four draw calls: bodies, heads, legs and shadows are each drawn many times over from one shape.
A ladder now stands on the far bank of the river, straight ahead of where every visit begins, rising out of sight into light, with angels going up and down it.
At its foot stands the stone Jacob set up for a pillar, with oil on its top.
Walk into its foot and he climbs, and light fills everything: this is the gate of heaven.
Heaven opens above: no night and no sun, only the light of the glory, with an emerald bow round about it.
A sea of glass like crystal, and down the middle of a street of gold, the river of the water of life.
The Tree of Life stands on either side of the river, with twelve manner of fruits.
Round the glory, a great multitude which no man could number, as thousands of lights.

Along both banks stand the saints of the site's own calendar, robed in white, in the order of their feasts; draw near one and its name and feast day are given, and the day's saint waits at the head of the ladder.
Walk back to the head of the ladder and he climbs down again into the garden, whose clock stood still while he was away.
Each step on the sea of glass kindles fire in it: a ring of gold runs out round his foot through the glass, and fades.
And each step plucks a harp: walk toward the glory and the notes climb, come away from it and they fall, wander and they wander.
Stand still a while and he lifts up his hands, and his prayer rises before him as incense, a thread of golden smoke going up and away toward the glory.
Now and then thin threads of incense rise from among the saints as well, the prayers of saints going up before the light.

Keep still while it rises and heaven answers: a wave of light rolls out through the whole multitude, the glory brightens, and many voices sing Alleluia over the sound of many waters, and the word is given.
Leaves let go of the Tree of Life, flutter down onto the river and are carried down it past the saints toward the head of the ladder; walk along beside them and their word is given.
The incense is one draw call, every puff's rise worked out on the graphics chip; the leaves are one more; and the fire is painted by the glass's own shader, with no draw call of its own.
Tap the sky and he lies down on his back in the grass to look up into it; the view comes down beside his head and lifts with his eyes. Any tap or drag and he gets up again.
By day the great flock leaves its wandering and comes to wheel right over him as he lies, high up and filling the sky.
By night his eyes grow used to the dark: thousands more stars come out, and the Milky Way, with its dark rifts and its bright heart, right across the sky.
His eyes go in turn to each named sign the season sets high enough, and to the moon when she rides high, and each is named: Ash the Bear, Kesil Orion, Kimah the Pleiades, Yareach the moon.
Now and then a star in sight brightens and sings one high, glassy note.
Lying still, he draws the shyer creatures near, as when he sits by the water.
The garden's stars are soft and round now rather than square, and the signs' lines show a little more while he lies looking up.
The new stars and the Milky Way are two draw calls, drawn only by night (the Milky Way only while he lies looking up), so nothing new is drawn in the garden's opening view.
The holy city's wall now stands foursquare round all of heaven, great and high, out past where the walk can reach, its far sides fading into the gold air.

Its foundations are twelve courses of precious stones, jasper at the foot up through sapphire, emerald and topaz to amethyst at the top, each stone catching the light in its own time, with small glints coming and going on them up close; above them the wall is clear jasper, coped with gold.

Three gates on every side, twelve in all, each one a single pearl whose nacre plays rose, gold and sea-green as you move, and every one standing open, with light pouring in through it and across the glass.
Over each gate an angel stands as a light, breathing slowly.

Through every gate the nations walk in: a slow procession of small golden lights comes in at each gate and walks on toward the glory, parting round Adam where he stands in their way and closing again behind him.
From the south side's middle gate, just east of the street behind the head of the ladder, they walk on north beside the saints toward the Tree of Life.
That gate is within his reach: stand on its threshold and the pearl and the light in its way brighten, and its word is given: Sha'ar, the gates of it shall not be shut at all by day.

The whole city is four draw calls (the wall with its foundations, the twelve pearls, the light in the gates, and the travellers with the lights over the gates), and the travellers are moved wholly in their shader; the stones' joints and glints are only worked out near enough to be seen.

Water a sapling: carried water poured at the roots of a young tree planted by the river, which grows a little with every visit he tends it (Isaiah 61:3)
Doves washing at the river's edge, dipping and shaking out their wings in the shallows by the bank (Song of Solomon 5:12)

The healing of the nations: the travellers who come up the street to the Tree of Life each take a leaf from it and carry it back out through the gates, glowing green, to the nations beyond (Revelation 22:2)
